question: Evaluate $\int \sqrt{9-x^2}\,dx$ by making a suitable trigonometric substitution and simplifying the resulting expression completely in terms of $x$.
explanation:
The expression $\sqrt{9-x^2}$ suggests the substitution $x=3\sin\theta$. Then

$$dx=3\cos\theta\,d\theta$$

and

$$\sqrt{9-x^2}=\sqrt{9-9\sin^2\theta}=3\cos\theta$$

Therefore,

$$\int \sqrt{9-x^2}\,dx=\int \left(3\cos\theta\right)\left(3\cos\theta\right)d\theta$$

$$=9\int \cos^2\theta\,d\theta$$

Using $\cos^2\theta=\frac{1+\cos2\theta}{2}$,

$$9\int \cos^2\theta\,d\theta=\frac{9}{2}\int \left(1+\cos2\theta\right)d\theta$$

$$=\frac{9}{2}\left(\theta+\frac{\sin2\theta}{2}\right)+C$$

Since $x=3\sin\theta$, we have

$$\theta=\sin^{-1}\left(\frac{x}{3}\right)$$

Also, $\sin\theta=\frac{x}{3}$ and $\cos\theta=\frac{\sqrt{9-x^2}}{3}$. Hence,

$$\sin2\theta=2\sin\theta\cos\theta=\frac{2x\sqrt{9-x^2}}{9}$$

Substituting these values,

$$\int \sqrt{9-x^2}\,dx=\frac{9}{2}\sin^{-1}\left(\frac{x}{3}\right)+\frac{9}{4}\left(\frac{2x\sqrt{9-x^2}}{9}\right)+C$$

$$=\frac{x}{2}\sqrt{9-x^2}+\frac{9}{2}\sin^{-1}\left(\frac{x}{3}\right)+C$$

Therefore, the required integral is $\frac{x}{2}\sqrt{9-x^2}+\frac{9}{2}\sin^{-1}\left(\frac{x}{3}\right)+C$.
